stories.headline: Democrats Promise to Investigate SpaceX. The Catch, Per Axios: The Government “Has No Replacement.”
stories.deck: Musk’s rockets flew roughly 90% of U.S. orbital launches this year. His case: SpaceX is “BOTH the best product AND the lowest price!”
stories.body:
The new Democratic majority is vowing a slew of investigations into Elon Musk’s companies, Axios reports. One Senate aide counted the Republican hearings on SpaceX so far: “Zero.”

Then Axios lays out the catch. For critical military and space missions, “the government has no replacement for SpaceX — and likely won’t for years.” SpaceX flew nearly 94% of U.S. orbital launches last year and roughly 90% so far in 2026, per American Enterprise Institute data.

Musk’s pitch: SpaceX contracts are “BOTH the best product AND the lowest price!”

Investigate away. Somebody still has to fly the rockets.

stories.headline: The Times Said Trump Called C-SPAN “Apparently Without Notice.” The Correction: “Mr. Trump Was Invited to Call In.”
stories.deck: The line ran in a news analysis on Trump’s “chaotic greatest hits.” The fix came after Trump called it out overnight. A syndicated copy still runs the old line.
stories.body:
A New York Times news analysis on Trump’s “chaotic greatest hits” said he called into the premiere of a C-SPAN show “apparently without notice.”

Early Wednesday, Trump posted that it was “a fully scheduled call, as a favor to C-Span, set up through White House Communications.”

The Times then appended a correction: “Due to an editing error, an earlier version of this story misstated the circumstances of a call President Trump made to C-SPAN. Mr. Trump was invited to call in. He did not call in unannounced.”

SpaceX and Tesla are progressing in merger negotiations, and a deal could be announced as early as December, Bloomberg News reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter, according to Reuters.

He says he missed a flight, got turned away from the partner party and won three grand off camera, figures he later contradicted. On camera, he lost a Stake blackjack hand, handed a photographer he’d just met $50 instead, ordered onion-loaded hot dogs he named “the Chernobyl,” and rode in the stranger’s car to the rental, where Panda was eating Raising Cane’s. stories.deck: CobbRuvs’ nine-hour Toronto marathon went condo kitchen, freezing sightseeing walk, then Stake, ending on a $12 parlay he says pays $2,300.

stories.headline: JPMorgan Said It Never Debanks for Politics. Here’s What the Federal Regulator Found.
stories.deck: A bank’s CEO can say anything at a shareholder meeting. A watch list is harder to argue with.
stories.body:
May 21, 2019, JPMorgan’s shareholder meeting. Jamie Dimon: “We have not and do not debank people because of their political views.”

Oct. 14, 2026: the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found that from 2020 to September 2025, all nine of the largest banks had such policies.

JPMorgan’s payment company flagged “MAGA, Make America Great, and America First.” An employee scrubbed “right wing” and “religious” from a nonprofit’s file.

To be fair: one bank turned away a group whose political arm endorsed only Democrats. The weight of the examples is not close.

stories.headline: Letitia James Unveils Justice System That Cuts Out the Middleman: the Facts and the Law
stories.deck: New York’s top law enforcement officer, on camera: “You don’t have to look at the facts and the law.”
stories.body:
Oct. 8, the New York attorney general debate on Spectrum News NY1. The topic was prediction markets. Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor, said she has to look at the facts and the law.

Attorney General Letitia James corrected her: “You don’t have to look at the facts and the law. All you have to do is study what they do. It is illegal in the state of New York, period.”

Asked to name a past attorney general she admires, James paused. She later named Bob Abrams.

The job is looking at the facts and the law.

stories.headline: The Boston Globe Finally Unmasked the Man Behind Mass Daily News
stories.deck: He is a software engineer. He has a laptop. Readers follow him. The Globe ran a profile.
stories.body:
Oct. 10: the Boston Globe combed through public records and named the man behind Mass Daily News. Simon Pacheco, 36, a Boston software engineer. He runs the site alone, nights and weekends.

The Globe’s case: the site is largely AI-written, and its posts attack Mayor Michelle Wu.

The Globe’s own admission: the site “has broken some news, including the arrest of a City Hall employee that the Globe subsequently reported on.”

One man and a phone beat the Globe to a City Hall arrest. The Globe responded by finding out his name.
